reason: One 48-byte string was sampled during the rounded-fill trace, with no allocating callee resolved below DrawRectangle. This isolated tick does not establish a per-draw cost. Allocation-counter tests measured zero managed bytes across 1,000 warmed solid and rounded fills, including small gradients.

One 48-byte string was sampled with no allocating callee resolved below DrawGlyphRun. This isolated tick does not establish a per-draw cost. A separate allocation-counter test checks warmed repeated glyph draws.
Avalonia's shaping contract returns an owned layout buffer. Each shaping request creates this wrapper; retained glyph runs reuse the result for drawing.
The shaped layout owns a wrapper around pooled glyph storage. The wrapper is created during shaping, while the glyph array is reused from Avalonia's pool.
Avalonia retains the shaped glyph storage through a reference wrapper so layout slices can share its lifetime. This runs during shaping, not each retained draw.
The layout buffer's reference counter releases its pooled glyph storage when the final layout slice is disposed.
Avalonia's ILockedFramebuffer contract returns a disposable lock object. A tile is locked once, while the render thread writes its pixels; drawing a cached tile does not lock it.

SKImage.FromPixels wraps the tile's pixels in a pixmap instead of copying 1 MB per tile. It runs on a tile's first draw after a write; later frames reuse the cached image (DrawOneToOne allocates nothing).
The image that shares the tile's pixels, created on the first draw after a write and cached until the next write.
SkiaSharp registers each new native wrapper in its handle table with a weak reference. One per image snapshot, once per written tile.
SkiaSharp's FromPixels keeps the pixmap alive through a release callback closure. One per image snapshot, once per written tile.
SkiaSharp's handle table entry for a new native wrapper. One per image snapshot, once per written tile.
Assigning a preview sheet changes its image width and height. Avalonia creates property notifications for layout. This runs when a sheet is assigned or recycled.
Assigning a preview sheet changes its caption. Avalonia creates a text property notification. This runs when the caption changes.
Changing the preview view model updates the control's data context. Avalonia creates a property notification for the new context.
ReactiveUI notifies subscribers when the preview view model changes. Each assigned sheet triggers this notification.
Opening document properties creates a file-info object, display strings and property entries in a list. The dialog owns this snapshot.
The properties dialog formats the file size as a display string. Its units array is local to that conversion.
Each metadata value shown by the properties dialog becomes one entry in its snapshot.
Importing a signature copies the source pixels into an owned buffer. It runs when the user imports an image.
A visible signature becomes one immutable image record. Cropping also creates an exact-sized pixel buffer. Full-size images reuse the owned source buffer.
The first call to each native entry point probes absolute library paths. This builds path strings during native binding. Later calls use the bound entry point.
Each submitted print job builds its CUPS option array and formats its copy count. These options carry paper, colour and duplex binding to the printer.
Opening a document creates its PdfiumDocument, once per file opened.
Opening a document wraps PDFium's document in one SafeHandle so it is always closed, once per file opened.
Opening a document opens its file handle and the read structure PDFium keeps for the document's life, once per file opened.
A newly opened document sets up its page sizes, its page and annotation caches and its form environment, once per file opened.
The first use of a page loads it into a PdfiumPage, kept in the document's page cache, so it happens once per page while the document stays open.
Search in Folder keeps each match with its snippet (the result) and lists the file's matches; it runs off the UI thread once per file searched.
The measurement's description is the result shown in the Measure bar and beside the shape; one string per pointer move while measuring.
Reading a drawing's declared scale parses the file's cross-reference data and its viewport and measure dictionaries, once per page when measuring starts on it.
The replacements of the sentence normalizer read their match groups and build the spoken words, once per sentence before it is phonemized; see TextNormalizer.

Normalizing a sentence for the voice rewrites it with generated regular expressions, each replacement making a new string, once per sentence before it is phonemized. Synthesizing the sentence takes hundreds of milliseconds, so this is negligible.

Reading a tagged page's structure tree makes one TaggedBlock (with its character index array) per element, which is the result, and remembers which marked content it has used. It runs once per page when Focus Mode or Read Aloud first reads it; ReadingDocument caches the page.
The per-page cache of whether each font is bold grows its buckets when a page uses a new font; see GetCharacters.
A string read from PDFium, such as an outline title or a figure's alternative text, is the result; one per call.
A string read from PDFium, such as an outline title or a figure's alternative text, is the result; one per call.
Reading a tagged page groups its characters by marked content id in a dictionary of index lists, once per page; ReadingDocument caches the result.
Reading a tagged page creates the structure walker and its used-id set once per page; ReadingDocument caches the result.
An element's /ActualText or a figure's /Alt text is read into a string only when the element has one; it becomes the block's text.

Reading a page's characters remembers whether each of its fonts is bold, so each font's name is read once per page rather than once per character. Runs once per page when its reading order is worked out.
The extracted text is the result; one string per call, sized exactly.

Checking a signature decodes the CMS and builds the certificate chain with System.Security.Cryptography, which allocates, and SignedCms needs the signed bytes as one array. It runs only when the user asks to check signatures.

The page and strip pixel buffers are rented from ArrayPool<byte>.Shared. The pool allocates them the first time a page is recognised (or after it trims idle buffers on a gen 2 GC); later pages reuse them. Seen once per trace.
Finding a language's data builds one path string per folder and language checked, because File.Exists takes a string. It runs once each time Recognise Text is pressed, never per page.
Reading TESSDATA_PREFIX returns a new string. It runs once each time Recognise Text is pressed, never per page.

Checking a downloaded language or voice file reads its size through FileInfo and builds the path of its recorded hash. It runs when Recognise Text is pressed or a download starts, not while reading or rendering.
Listing the language packs still to download builds each pack's path and returns a new list of the missing packs. It runs when Recognise Text is pressed or a download starts.

The download's copy buffer is rented from ArrayPool<byte>.Shared. The pool allocates a buffer when the download continues on a core whose cache is still empty; later downloads on that core reuse it. A download runs only when the person asks for a language.
Starting a language download builds the Refit request and its User-Agent header inside System.Net.Http. It happens once per language downloaded.
Splitting the language setting, for example eng+deu, returns a new list of codes. It runs when Recognise Text is pressed or Preferences opens.

Each recognised word becomes a string (the result), and Tesseract's result iterator is wrapped in one SafeHandle per page. Recognition itself takes hundreds of milliseconds in Tesseract's native code.
The first time a LibraryImport returns a given SafeHandle type, the generated marshaller creates it with new T(), which builds the runtime's per-type activator cache once for the life of the process.

The layout is the result: one immutable object with arrays sized exactly to the pages and rows. It is built only when the zoom, arrangement, rotation or viewport size changes, never while scrolling; lookups on it allocate nothing.

Exporting pages for printing opens new native documents (the copy and, for several pages per sheet, the sheets) and each page whose annotations are left out; each is owned by one small SafeHandle so it is always closed. Exporting runs when print settings change, never while viewing.

Signing writes a new file: the original bytes plus an incremental update built as text, the cross-reference data it reads (inflated object and cross-reference streams), and a CMS signature from System.Security.Cryptography over the signed bytes, which SignedCms needs as one array. A damaged file also gets its cross-reference entries rebuilt by scanning (PdfRepair) and a full cross-reference stream. It runs once, when the user signs.

Reading layers parses the file's structure and returns new layer records; switching a layer writes a new copy of the file (the original bytes plus a small update with the new default visibility). Both run when the layers panel opens or a box is ticked, never while scrolling.

Switching a layer rebuilds the in-memory copy pages are drawn from: the file's bytes, the layers left hidden and the copy itself. Once per tick of a layer box; drawing from the copy allocates nothing.
Switching a layer reads the document's current bytes (from the file, or with unsaved edits written in) to build the copy pages are drawn from. Once per tick of a layer box.
A layer's visibility is an immutable record, replaced when its box is ticked.
The layer view's page cache and the SafeHandles owning its native copy and pages, created when a layer is switched; reused for every page drawn afterwards.
The SafeHandle owning the native memory that holds the layer view's copy, one per switch.

Phonemizing runs once per sentence read aloud, while the previous sentence plays. Each word is cut out as a string to look it up in the pronunciation dictionary (and lower-cased when it is not listed as written), and the phonemes are the returned string. The token list and output builder are reused between sentences; a trace can still show the reused builder growing its chunks.
Numbers in a sentence are said as words, for example 1984 as 'nineteen eighty four'; the words are a new string per number, made only for sentences that contain digits.
Preparing a sentence for the voice returns it as a new string with line breaks joined; one per sentence read aloud, built in a StringBuilder sized to the sentence.
The SSML document sent to Azure for one sentence is the result; one string per sentence, with the text escaped.
The samples are the returned audio for one sentence, handed to the sound output; one array per sentence, sized exactly.

Reading order runs once per page, when the page is first read aloud or shown in Focus Mode, and the result is kept by ReadingDocument. It builds a line object per line of text, a block object per paragraph, the joined text of each block with the page character index of every character (the map that lets the spoken sentence be highlighted on the page), and the lists the XY-cut groups blocks into; all proportional to the page's text.
Flattening a page for Read Aloud returns its text and the matching character map, one string and one int array per page read, sized exactly.
Reading a page's characters loads PDFium's text page the first time it is used; the list it fills is the caller's and is reused.

MeloTTS's front end runs once per sentence read aloud, while the previous sentence plays. BERT's cleaning lower-cases and decomposes the sentence into new strings, and the reused cleaning buffer grows once to the longest sentence seen; the piece ids, phones and model input lists are reused between sentences.
The caller's reused list of guessed phones grows once to the longest guess; the phone names themselves are shared strings and the network's state is reused.

Linking replies runs once per save of a document that gained replies: it parses the saved file, gives inline annotations on pages with replies objects of their own, rewrites each reply with its /IRT reference, and returns the file with the update appended as a new array.

A comment's thread is read when the annotations list is refreshed: each reply's text, author and status are new strings in a new record, and the comment's name is read once to match replies saved before linking.
Reading an annotation's text value (contents, author, name or status) returns it as a new string; done when the list is refreshed, not while drawing.
Matching a reply to its comment reads the reply's pending comment name as a string; only replies added since the last save have one.
Replying writes the reply's name, the comment it answers and its modification date; the name is a new string per reply.
Each reply, and a comment the first time it is replied to, gets a unique name as a new string.
Printing a booklet lists the pages in booklet order, once per print preview or print; the booklet step is inlined into the export.
The booklet page order's backing array, sized to the sheets, once per print preview or print.
The booklet page order, sized to the sheets, once per print preview or print.
The benchmark's local timestamp authority, standing in for a remote one: it builds and signs each token. The app makes none of these allocations; its tokens come from the network.
The document security store is read once when the user checks a document's signatures: the file's structure, the store's certificate streams, and a certificate object for each.
Checking a signature runs when the user asks to see the signatures: it reads the signed bytes, decodes the CMS and any timestamp token, and builds certificate chains.
Signing or timestamping writes a new copy of the file with an incremental update, the CMS signature or token, and its hex form; once per signature.
Field scripts are recognised once, when a form is first edited: the regular expressions' matches, the arguments and field names as strings, and the script record.
Evaluating a calculation reads each field name as a string to look its value up; once per calculated field per edit.
Formatting or reading a number builds the text, with its separators and currency, as new strings; once per field per edit.
Formatting or reading a date converts the field's format into a pattern string; once per date field per edit.
Running a script works on new strings for the value it formats or checks, and a closure for a calculation's field lookups; once per field per edit.
Reading a form's scripts, once when it is first edited: each widget's name and action scripts as strings, and its scripts record.
Reading a form's scripts, once when it is first edited: the list of scripted fields grows.
A form field's name, value or script is read from PDFium as a new string; when fields are listed after an edit, or scripts are read once.
Following a link to another file builds that file's full path, once per click on the link. Nothing here runs while pages draw.
A link written with the other system's folder separators is rewritten once per click so the file can be found; a path that already uses this system's separators is returned as it is.
Closing a tab at a new page records one small entry in the settings; an unchanged newest entry is kept without allocating.
The message about content that cannot be shown is built once per combination of parts and then reused for every document.
Judging whether a field's script is one PdfViewerLite runs means reading the script text, once per field in the background check made when a document opens.

The corrections are returned in a new list of five, the list and its array. Copying them into an array of their exact count saved the list but measured 30 to 40 ns slower. Corrections are looked up only when the reader opens the menu on a misspelled word.
Loading a word list reads each word into a set, once per spell checker, when spell checking first starts.
The correction index is built once per word list, the first time a correction is asked for: the lower-case words, the per-word lookup marks and the hash directory.
Building the correction index makes one packed entry per word delete and a count per hash bucket, once per word list; the entries are dropped once grouped.
Building the correction index makes the key, start and posting arrays it keeps for the life of the spell checker, once per word list.
The first call to a native entry point probes the library path while binding it; one string for the life of the process.

Subsetting builds the new font program PDFium embeds: the renumbered glyph, metric and cmap tables and the assembled file. It runs when a text box in an installed font is written, once per 128-character block of new letters, never while typing or drawing. SubsetFont measures about 1 ms for a paragraph.
Lists the characters a font maps while its subset's cmap is built, once per subset.

The page and grey buffers are rented from ArrayPool and returned after each read. The trace shows two rents in the whole run, when the pool first fills; every later read reuses them. Detect itself allocates nothing.
Writing a text box makes its /DA, /DS and /RC values once per commit; PDFium copies them into the annotation. Reading a foreign FreeText makes its format once.
The format record kept with a text box: one string per commit, built in a stack buffer.
Reading a text box back to edit it makes the one TextFormat it returns. Settings are parsed into a struct first, so only the final record is allocated.
An installed font's family name read from a text box's record; built-in family names are reused.
A format with values out of range is copied once with usable ones; formats already in range are returned as they are.
The text and record strings stored in the annotation, once per commit.
The standard free text entries, written as one string of exact length once per commit.
Reading a text box returns its text and a TextBoxContent; the format record is decoded from a pooled buffer without a string.
Resolving the font for a commit returns the chosen TextFont and its base font name; loaded fonts and shapers are cached.
Finding an installed face returns a FontMatch describing the face and any synthetic bold or italic, once per commit.

When text boxes, replies or removed comments are pending, the save is written into a pooled buffer (PooledWriteStream, returned after the save) so AnnotationReplyLinks can turn kept entries into standard PDF. Saving is a user action, not a frame or keystroke.
PDFium's write callback copies each block into the stream the caller passed to Save; a growing MemoryStream destination grows here. Saves with pending work write into a pooled buffer instead.

The one exact copy of the saved file that the PDF reader parses to finish pending annotations, made only when the file has pending work. It replaced a growing MemoryStream, its ToArray copy and a concatenated copy of the file; the update is now written after the file instead.
The save buffer is rented from the shared pool and returned when the save ends; the trace shows the pool's first rent, which later saves reuse.

PdfSigner.Sign is inlined into the signing benchmark methods, so its allocations carry their names: the signed copy of the file and its incremental update as strings and bytes, and the CMS signature's ASN.1 reader and writer state. They are the same work the PdfSigner and PdfUpdateWriter entries explain, once per signature, which is a user action.

Opening a document reads its cross-reference table and page tree into an object store, a name table and dictionaries. The import benchmarks include this cost, so it is the baseline to subtract from them. Opening a file is a user action.

Reading an XFDF or FDF file builds the data model: one annotation object per annotation with its text as strings and its numbers as arrays. XFDF goes through XmlReader, which keeps its own node, attribute and name-table state and returns attribute values as strings. FDF goes through the PDF object parser into dictionaries and arrays. Reading a file is a user action, not a render path.

Exporting reads each annotation dictionary into the data model and writes it out. XFDF is written through XmlWriter, which formats attribute values as strings and keeps its own element, namespace and buffer state. FDF is written as PDF syntax into a pooled buffer and copied into the result array, with annotation dictionaries built as free objects. Exporting is a user action, not a render path.

Importing reads the file as described for the read benchmarks, then builds one annotation dictionary and object per annotation, queues them per page, links replies and pop-ups, and puts each page's array in place once. It also includes opening the fresh document, which the OpenOnly entry explains. Importing is a user action, not a render path.

Each operation opens a fresh document, so it pays every first-use cost once: the object store, name table, page tree and page objects; the page's first recording (interpreter, graphics state stack, Skia paths, picture recorder and picture); the text page and its characters; the annotation editor and the new highlight's dictionaries; the page tree read again because the edit drops the cached pages; and the compact save's cross-reference rows and one ZLib encoder per compressed stream. All of it is open, edit and save work, which are user actions; later tiles of the same page replay the cached picture without managed allocation.

The PDFium adapter's open, text page, annotation and save wrappers: the page size and annotation lists, the text string and the managed write buffer. Native memory is not traced. Open, edit and save are user actions, not a render path.

Inserting pages is an edit transaction: the transaction and its undo record, the page set and page tree read again after the edit, the copied page dictionaries and the rewritten page tree. The carrier objects and their lists are created once per insertion and find nothing to carry in a plain document. Inserting pages is a user action, not a render path.

Everything InsertPlain allocates, plus what the carried structures need: prepared annotation copies, the field nodes and their rebuilt dictionaries, the outline entries and their reserved objects, the named destination and embedded file name entries merged into new name tree leaves, the layer list, and the merged AcroForm, resources and catalog copies. Each is built once per insertion. Inserting pages is a user action, not a render path.

Extracting builds a new document: the builder's object list, the copied page and annotation objects, the same carried structures as InsertBook written into the new catalog, and the file bytes with compressed streams. Extracting pages is a user action, not a render path.

The carriers (forms, outlines, destinations, layers, files, text, context) build their working lists, dictionaries, arrays and reserved objects once per page copy, sized by what the copied pages reference. Copying pages is a user action, not a render path.
The carrier runs once per page copy and creates one object per structure it keeps, with the annotation list of each page and the merged catalog. Copying pages is a user action, not a render path.
Merging into a name tree reads the old entries, sorts old and new together and writes one leaf array, once per tree per page copy.
Comparing the form defaults of two documents builds the font rename table and the renamed default appearance string, once per page copy that carries fields.
Page labels are copied with a style table that keeps pages that shared a style in one run, and written as one number tree, once per page copy.
Copying objects between documents allocates the queue of objects still to copy and the copied dictionaries, arrays and stream data holders, once per object copied.
Rewriting the page tree after an insertion builds the list of old nodes and the new kids array, once per edit.
Committing an edit builds the undo record and the lists of changed objects and trailer entries, once per edit.
The edit transaction's touched-object set grows while a page edit records the objects it will be able to undo.
The edit transaction's before-state list grows to retain the original objects for undo.
Inserting pages allocates the carrier, the importer's queue, the reserved ids, the prepared annotation arrays and the page slots, once per insertion. Page editing is a user action, not a render path.
An edit allocates its transaction and the lists that record changed objects and trailer entries, once per edit.
Copying a page dictionary builds its copy once per inserted page.
Reading the source labels of the copied pages builds the label array and a decimal style, once per insertion.
Rebuilding the labels of the new page order builds the label array and a decimal style, once per insertion.
The label ranges are read once after an edit drops the cached ranges.
The page slots list is built once per page edit.
Writing the page tree after an edit builds the label list and the tree's working state, once per edit.
The page tree is read again after an edit drops the cached pages, building the page list and the traversal stack.
The page set is rebuilt after an edit drops the cached pages.
Reading the entries of a name tree for a merge builds the entry list once per tree.
Reading the source's layer state to copy it builds the group list and the sets of hidden and listed groups, once per page copy that reaches a layer.
Extracting pages reserves one object per page and keeps the prepared annotation arrays, once per extraction.
Copying objects into a new document allocates the queue of objects still to copy and the copied dictionaries, arrays and stream data holders, once per object copied.
The builder holds the new document's objects and writes them with compressed streams and a cross-reference table, once per extraction.
A new dictionary's key and value arrays, made for each dictionary a page copy builds; their size follows the entries the copied object holds.
Copying a dictionary for editing (an annotation, a field, the catalog or an outline root) allocates its key and value arrays, once per edited dictionary in a page copy.
A name the target has not seen is added to its name table, once per new name in a page copy.
A name tree key or field name is decoded to a string to compare names, once per name checked in a page copy.
The first copy of a page parses the source's objects that were not read yet, so arrays are allocated once per object.
The first copy of a page parses the source's objects that were not read yet, so dictionaries are allocated once per object.

Opening a file creates its byte source once per document: the mapped view and its accessor, or the stream source's 64 KiB page cache. The Memory source reads the whole file into one array by design (File.ReadAllBytes), which is why the Memory rows of the source benchmarks show the file size per open. Opening is a user action.
Opening reads the cross-reference table or streams into one entry array sized to the file's object count, and repair scans a damaged file once. Both run once per open, a user action.

The object store is created once per open with its object slot array, trailer and catalog. ReadStream and RootResolves load an object the first time it is used and keep it in the slot array, so each object is parsed once per document. Edits keep the edited copies until saved. None of this runs when a recorded tile is drawn.
Each document has one name table. The first spelling of a name not in the static known-name table is interned once and reused for every later use in that document.

Parsing an object builds its value: a PdfDictionary or PdfArray allocated once at its final size from the per-thread parse stack, its key and value arrays, and strings with escapes. Parsed objects are cached in the object store, so each is parsed once per document. Inline marked-content property lists are parsed when a page is recorded or its text read, which is once per page; warm tiles replay the recorded picture.
Builds a dictionary that the caller keeps: a parsed object, a clone for an edit, or a generated appearance resource. Runs when an object is first loaded or edited, not when a recorded tile is drawn.
Builds the number array of a generated annotation appearance (its bounding box or matrix). Appearances are generated once per annotation when the page is recorded.

Decode returns a text string as a .NET string and Encode returns the encoded bytes as a new array; both results belong to the caller (titles, outline entries, metadata, annotation text). They run when the caller asks for text, not when a tile is drawn.
Reading the page tree builds one page entry per page and the inherited attribute chain once per document, or again after an edit replaces the tree. It runs on open or first page access.
The page set holds the page array and the reverse lookup from object number to page index. It is built once per document and again after a page edit.

Document-level reads that return results the caller keeps or the document caches once: Create builds the document and its lazily filled caches, the page set and output intents are read once, and outline, link, URI, info, viewer preference and conformance reads return records and strings. RunContent creates one content interpreter with its graphics state, resource and marked-content stacks per content run, which happens once per text page build or raster scan, and the text page is cached. RunEdit and CurrentSlots copy the page slots for an undoable page edit. None of these run when a recorded tile is drawn.
Spells PDF names out as strings for the accessibility report, which returns them to the caller. The report is a user action.

The optional content configuration is read once per document: the group list, the radio button groups, the referenced group numbers and the hidden set. Toggling a layer copies the hidden set under the lock and publishes the new set, so render threads read a stable snapshot without locking; a toggle is a user action and costs one small set.

Recording a page or building its text page runs the content stream once: the interpreter, its path builders and stacks; one Skia path object per painted path, clip or shading (SkiaSharp wraps each detached path in a managed object and registers its handle); a font and colour space the first time a resource is used; the soft mask and transparency group state; and the marked-content stack. The recording is cached as a picture, so warm tiles replay it without managed allocation. When the device is the marked-content recorder, ShowCode, OpFill and the marked-content operators also grow the recorder's glyph list, text buffer and bounds table, which are the recording's result.

The document's render cache is created on the first render, and Decode and ToSkImage decode an image and wrap it in a Skia image once; the entry stays in the 64 MiB image cache until evicted. Large pixel arrays are placed on the pinned object heap and become Skia's own pixel memory, so the decode output is not copied.
The image cache's dictionary and recency list, created once per document on the first render.
The colour space, shading, pattern and soft mask caches, created once per document on the first render.

Recording a page into a picture, once per page while it stays in the renderer's picture cache (bounded by the memory the pictures hold, 128 MiB by default, and 32 pages): the picture recorder, the content device and the annotation pass. Warm tiles replay the picture and allocate nothing.
Draw allocates only when the page has no cached picture yet: it records the page and adds its cache entry. Warm tiles take the cached path and allocate nothing, as the warm tile benchmarks measure.

Adds a page's cache entry the first time the page is drawn, evicting the least recently used page beyond the page cap. The first use of a renderer also registers it, weakly, with its document so disposing the document releases the renderer's pictures.

Generates an appearance stream for an annotation that has none (square, circle, ink, markup, polygon, line, note): its content bytes, form dictionary and resources. This runs once per annotation when the page is recorded; the result is drawn into the cached picture.

The recording device's soft masks, transparency group stack and Skia paints, created while a page is recorded and released with the device. SkiaSharp registers each native handle in its handle table, which grows under this frame. Recording runs once per page.

Decoding an image returns its pixels (one gray byte, BGRA or alpha coverage) as a new array the size of the image. Arrays of 64 KiB or more are zeroed arrays on the pinned object heap that Skia then uses as its own pixel memory, so nothing is copied; smaller ones are copied into Skia. The gray table (256 bytes) and the unpacker tables are built once per image. Each image is decoded once while it stays in the cache. Scratch rows are rented from the shared or the bounded scratch pool; when a pool has no array of a size yet, the first rent allocates it under this frame.

Each JPEG 2000 decode builds its header model (coding style, quantization, tiles and tile parts), one block decoder per worker and the component planes' work items, and runs the code blocks and components with Parallel.For, whose task replicas and ranges are allocated per call. A decode runs once per image while it stays in the image cache. Plane buffers are pooled.

Each JBIG2 decode builds its segment list, region and symbol dictionary settings, symbol stores and arithmetic contexts: a few hundred bytes to a few kilobytes per page decode. Bitmaps are pooled. A decode runs once per image while it stays in the image cache.
The default decode array of an image's colour space, built once per image decode.
A shading or transfer function is parsed into its coefficient arrays once, when the shading is first used, and cached with the shading.
A shading's Skia shader and its colour stops are built once and cached with the shading in the document's render cache.

Loading a font, once per font dictionary per document: its descriptor, program and tables, encoding and widths, glyph name text (one-character texts are shared across fonts), name words for system font matching, and the substitute face. Glyph outlines are built the first time a code is drawn and kept in the font's outline cache, in pages of 256 slots. Predefined CMaps and CID-to-Unicode tables are read from the assembly once per process. Warm text tiles, width and text lookups and CMap lookups allocate nothing.

Building a text page creates the page's result: its character array, line and word index arrays, the page text string and segments, and one marks record each time the open marked-content levels change. Text pages are cached per document (16 pages, least recently used first), and warm find and hit test allocate nothing.

Structure reads return their results: the structure tree's elements and kids, the role map chain, the marked-content recording of a page (glyphs, text and bounds per MCID), tagged nodes, and the inferred layout's lines, columns and paragraphs. They run when a reader asks for structure, once per page or document, not when a tile is drawn.

The accessibility report is a user action that returns a report: one page record per page, one finding per problem with its message, counts, the structure scan's element map and visited set, and page classification strings.
The conformance report is a user action that returns a report: the PDF/A claim, the output intents and one observation per page and font.
The raster report returns one page record per page and one image record per scanned image with its filter names. It is a user action that walks the whole document once.
XFDF and FDF import and export build the annotation data model and the written file; see the interchange benchmark entries. These are user actions, not a render path.
Editing annotations creates the new annotation dictionaries, their text, date and colour values and the page's new /Annots array. Editing is a user action.
A page edit rewrites the page tree: it collects the nodes, copies inherited attributes into moved pages and writes new Kids arrays, all inside one undoable transaction. Editing is a user action.
Writing an OCR text layer adds new content streams and wraps the page's contents in a new array. It is a user action.

Optimising is a user action that rewrites the whole file once. Each run opens a working copy, so every object is parsed again (OptimizerGraph.Visit inlines those loads) and the reachable-object graph, renumbering map and cross-reference rows are built at the file's size. Duplicate finding keeps one content hash per stream; font subsetting runs each page's content once to collect glyphs and builds the subset font's tables and file as new arrays; image recoding produces the new JPEG or bilevel data; the writer compresses object streams with one ZLib encoder each; the report lists every action and skip. None of it runs while viewing or rendering.

Reading an XMP packet goes through a forward-only XmlReader, which keeps its own node, namespace and name-table state and returns element text as strings. The optimiser reads the packet once per run to keep or update document metadata; viewers read it once per document.

Saving collects the reachable objects, writes the cross-reference rows, computes the file ID and compresses streams with one ZLib encoder per stream. The saved bytes are returned to the caller. Saving is a user action.
Opening a document through the adapter creates the library document and its wrapper. Opening is a user action.

The adapter converts library results into the app's records: the wrapper's state on open, outline items, links and viewer rectangles. RenderNative creates the document's renderer entry on the first render; later tiles find it and allocate nothing, as the warm tile benchmarks measure.
The adapter's annotation editor: its name table, the new markup's dictionaries and the text layer's font list. Annotation and text layer edits are user actions.
The annotation name index, created once per annotation editor.
The tagged block walker and character map build the reading order blocks the app asks for, once per page.

The PDFium adapter's open, navigation and text wrappers, measured as the comparison baseline: native handles, outline and link lists, label and URI strings. Native memory is not traced. These run on open or on user actions.

Library code inlined into a HyperPDF benchmark method allocates under the benchmark's name. Each such site is the same first-use or result work the library entries explain: opening documents and creating renderers in cold benchmarks, decoder state in the codec benchmarks, the returned encoded bytes, image, report or page records, and the copied hidden set of a layer toggle. Every warm render, text query, font lookup, colour and syntax benchmark measures zero.
Library code inlined into the accessibility report benchmark: opening the document and the report's result records, as the accessibility entry explains.
Mapping the app's settings to the library's options and the library's report to the app's creates the option record, the report record and its lists. Once per run, when the user clicks Save a Copy.
Taking the snapshot lists the pages that hold annotations removed but kept, so they can be left out of the copy and put back. Once per run, only when such annotations exist.
Benchmark harness code: the output stream that stops the run at its first write, and the mapping calls the benchmark makes on purpose. Not shipped.
One 64-byte context per open holds the cancellation token, recovery switches and the repair log, so a document can say whether it was repaired. Opening is a user action, not a render path.
The repair log is created on the first report only, so a clean open allocates none of it. A damaged open allocates the log list, its de-duplication set and their backing arrays once.
The de-duplication set of the repair log, created with the log on the first report of a damaged open.
The backing array of the repair log's de-duplication set, created on the first report of a damaged open.

Reading the notices decodes the UTF-8 file to a string, then builds the data model: one entry per component with its licence text as a string, a field dictionary per component, and the group lists. It runs once, when the user opens the Licences window, and is not a render path.

Decoding the UTF-8 notices file to one string, which the compiler inlines into the caller; the string holds the whole file (about 800 KB for 70 components). It happens once, when the user opens the Licences window, and is not a render path.

The reader keeps a string builder for the licence text and a field dictionary for each component, and fills the entry and group lists. It runs once, when the user opens the Licences window, and is not a render path.

Reads one bundled Foxit face the first time a document needs it: the resource stream and its name, a byte array of the face's CFF data (about 15 to 30 KB, kept by the parsed program for its lifetime), the CffProgram, the glyph source and the face object. The face is cached for the process, so this happens at most once per face and never while rendering.
Parsing a bundled face builds its charset, encoding and private dictionary tables once, when the face is first read. The program is cached for the process and never rebuilt while rendering.

Reading a page builds the object model the editor works on: one object per painted operation, a glyph array and a Unicode string for each text object, path segments, marks and the clip chain, and the parser's own state stack. Writing it again builds one byte array per text show so the TJ array can be rewritten and, in Preserve mode, one output buffer. Page object parsing and regeneration are editing actions that run once per edit. The render hot path does not call them.

Applying a redaction opens a working copy, reads each marked page into objects, rewrites the content, blanks image pixels, rewrites the ToUnicode maps, prunes resources, scrubs metadata and builds the overlay. Each step allocates its model, its decoded buffers and its rewritten streams. Applying is a user action that ends in a save. The render hot path does not call it.
Inlined library calls carry the benchmark's name: opening the document, applying the redaction and writing the saved copy to the output stream. The pages and the picture are built once in setup.
Inlined library calls carry the benchmark's name: the byte array a regenerate returns, and the objects an edit benchmark parses before it changes them.

Async load-ahead of a stream or file source. When a read really waits, the compiler's state machine is boxed once and a continuation is queued; a source whose pages are cached, and every mapped or in-memory source, completes without either.
One async read of a run of cache pages: a pooled run buffer (rented, returned in the same call) and the state machine box and continuation of the awaited read.
The awaited read of the file or stream: the box of the framework's own async read and the continuation that resumes after it.
Waiting for the stream's turn when another async load holds it; allocates only on contention.

A walk that loads a page's objects ahead of use: the walk's sets and lists, the merged range list and the walk's state machine. Made once per page and cache generation, then skipped while nothing is evicted; the per-dictionary mark is a one-off entry in a ConditionalWeakTable.

Cold async opening walks the page-tree references once per source and cache generation. The walk allocates visited sets, frontier lists and sorted byte ranges. On the 928-page source benchmark the largest sampled groups were about 44 KB of hash entries, 24 KB of object IDs and 30 KB of ranges per open. They are not part of warm page or tile replay.

The compiler-generated async prefetch methods allocate a state-machine box and continuations when file reads suspend. The walk also creates its frontier once per cold open. Warm prefetch hits return a completed ValueTask without these objects.
The prefetch mark is created once for each page or tree dictionary when async load-ahead first visits it; a cached generation reuses the mark.

Cold async prefetch sorts cross-reference offsets to estimate object byte extents. The 928-page benchmark allocated an approximately 258 KB long array and one list per open. It is built once for the source and is not used in warm replay.

On .NET 10 the Flate decoder uses a ZLibStream, DeflateStream, inflater and tracking wrapper for each decoded compressed stream. The 928-page cold-open benchmark decodes two such streams per open. The .NET 11 span decoder does not create these wrappers.
Opening with a cancellable token: the options copy that carries the token, plus the state machine box and continuations of the awaited loads. One set per open.
The async search walk: the iterator's state machine, the reused match list, and one match array for each page that has a match.
The async text walk: the iterator's state machine, once per walk.
Async form whose load-ahead really waited: the state machine box and continuation. Skipped, with no allocation, once the page is loaded; the allocation test checks that.
Slow path of GetPageAsync, taken only when the load-ahead really waited: state machine box and continuation.
Slow path of GetTextPageAsync, taken only when the load-ahead really waited: state machine box and continuation.
Slow path of GetOutlineAsync, taken only when the load-ahead really waited: state machine box and continuation.
Slow path of GetLinksAsync, taken only when the load-ahead really waited: state machine box and continuation.
Slow path of ScanAnnotationsAsync, taken only when the load-ahead really waited: state machine box and continuation.
Async save: the state machine box and continuation of the awaited copy and write, one set per save.
Slow path of RenderAsync, taken only when the load-ahead really waited: state machine box and continuation.
Async render whose load-ahead really waited: the slow path's state machine box and continuation. The fast path allocates nothing; the allocation test checks that.
The sorted object offsets used to find the bytes an object spans, built once per store on the first load-ahead of an object graph.
The benchmark harness: the opened-document wrapper, the delegates and tasks that start parallel renders, the task array and the throttled streams. Not library allocations.
Caching a freshly decoded image, once per image while it stays in the 64 MiB image cache: its map entry, recency node and the growth of the map. Never runs when a recorded tile is drawn.
The per-entry lock of a freshly decoded image, once per image while it stays in the image cache.

The record of one image decode in progress, made once per image that is not cached so a second thread waits for it instead of decoding again. A thread that waits for another thread's decode adds the monitor state it sleeps on; the task for async waiters exists only when one waits. Never runs for a cached image or when a recorded tile is drawn.
The list of images a page's picture drew, published once per recorded picture so renders can read it without a lock.

Adding up the picture cache's memory counts each shared image once, using a scratch set that grows to the number of distinct images. It runs only after a render recorded a picture, never when a recorded tile is drawn.

An object stream (or cross-reference stream) is decoded into one exact-size array. The store keeps only the last 8 decoded object streams within 4 MiB, so a stream that was evicted is decoded again the next time one of its unparsed objects is read. Each object is still parsed once per document, so this is a first-read cost, not a render cost.

Reading an object stream's header builds its object-number and offset arrays and the index that holds them next to the decoded data. It runs once per decode of an object stream, which is again after the bounded cache evicted it, and never when a recorded tile is drawn.
One 64-byte context per open holds the cancellation token, the recovery switches and the repair log, so a document can report whether it was repaired. Opening is a user action, not a render path.

Generates an appearance stream for an annotation that has none (square, circle, ink, markup, polygon, line, note): its content bytes, form dictionary and resources. This runs once per annotation when the page is recorded; the result is drawn into the cached picture.

Generates an appearance stream for an annotation that has none (square, circle, ink, markup, polygon, line, note): its content bytes, form dictionary and resources. This runs once per annotation when the page is recorded; the result is drawn into the cached picture.

Generates an appearance stream for an annotation that has none (square, circle, ink, markup, polygon, line, note): its content bytes, form dictionary and resources. This runs once per annotation when the page is recorded; the result is drawn into the cached picture.

Generates an appearance stream for an annotation that has none (square, circle, ink, markup, polygon, line, note): its content bytes, form dictionary and resources. This runs once per annotation when the page is recorded; the result is drawn into the cached picture.

Regenerating a form appearance writes its retained content bytes, form stream, bounding box, matrix and resource dictionaries. Compression creates encoder state. This is an edit operation; warm rendering draws the recorded appearance.

Regenerating text and choice appearances formats content operands and font names, splits multiline text into line records and writes the new appearance. These strings, line arrays and scratch lists occur during edits, never when a warmed tile is drawn.
Generating a button mark creates its appearance operands and glyph bytes before the result is saved in the widget's appearance stream. This runs during filling or regeneration, not warm rendering.
A form edit parses the field's default-appearance string into a font, size and colour record. Decoding names and formatting stroke colours creates strings and builder buffers for the new appearance.

Form appearance generation resolves the selected font and encoding, splits supplied text into Unicode runes, and creates encoded glyph bytes and width arrays. The resulting codes feed the new appearance; warm rendering does not run this editor path.
Resolving a field for an edit collects its widget controls into a list of control records, including direct controls and referenced widgets.

An undoable form edit clones changed dictionaries and collects original-to-copy mappings. Committing enumerates those copies and writes their replacement objects, preserving the original revision for undo.

Regenerating widgets creates one form-edit transaction and the rewritten appearance data for each resolved control. These objects support the edit and undo; the warmed render path uses cached pictures.
Resolving a form field for reading or filling creates its inherited attributes, control list and resolved widget record. Form inspection and editing run outside warmed rendering.
Filling a checkbox creates an undoable form edit and rewrites its checked state and appearance references.
A checkbox without an on-state appearance gets a new appearance dictionary and generated mark stream when it is filled.
Writing a button value creates the PDF value and state names stored in its field and widget dictionaries during filling.
Reading calculation order tracks visited field names in a hash set to omit duplicates. The set and its entry and index arrays are scratch for this form-order query.
Reading tab order collects widget sort keys in a list and its backing array, then appends their indexes to the caller's output. These keys preserve row, column or structure order during the query.

Resetting a field creates a form-edit builder, its replacement dictionary mappings and cloned field or widget dictionaries. The builder commits the default value and regenerated appearances as one field update.
Regenerating widgets creates one form-edit builder and the rewritten appearance data for each resolved control. These objects support the edit; warmed rendering uses cached pictures.
Resolving a form field for reading or filling creates its inherited attributes, control list and resolved widget record. Form inspection and editing run outside warmed rendering.
Filling a checkbox creates a form-edit builder and rewrites its checked state and appearance references.
A checkbox without an on-state appearance gets a new appearance dictionary and generated mark stream when it is filled.
Writing a button value creates the PDF value and state names stored in its field and widget dictionaries during filling.
Reading calculation order tracks visited field names in a hash set to omit duplicates. The set and its entry and index arrays are scratch for this form-order query.
Reading tab order collects widget sort keys in a list and its backing array, then appends their indexes to the caller's output. These keys preserve row, column or structure order during the query.

Resetting a field creates a form-edit builder, its replacement dictionary mappings and cloned field or widget dictionaries. The builder commits the default value and regenerated appearances as one field update.
Resolving form field flags reads the field type spelling into a string for edit dispatch.
Resolving a field constructs its full name from the parent chain for the returned form-field record.
Regenerating a choice field builds option-value counts and decoded strings to check that selected indices agree with the field values before highlighting rows.

Writing a compressed stream creates an encoder and retained compressed bytes. The .NET 10 fallback also creates MemoryStream, ZLibStream and deflater state. Compression is a save/edit operation, never a warmed tile draw.
A newly written stream sets its dictionary's Length entry. Growing that dictionary's value storage and name lookup creates amortised value and index arrays when the appearance is finalized.
Each newly opened document creates the lock protecting its diagnostic log. This accompanies the open context and does not run on warmed rendering.

A page action copies the selected indexes before awaiting resource loads. It creates an edit transaction, its open-transaction guard and lists of original objects and trailer entries for undo. Inlined page validation and cache rebuilds also create integer selections and visited sets. These allocations belong to the user-requested edit and its undo history; warmed reading and rendering do not enter ApplyAsync.

Runtime async reports the page action directly on .NET 11. The action freezes selected indexes, starts an undoable edit transaction and its guard, records original objects and trailer entries, and validates or rebuilds page selections using integer arrays and visited sets. These allocations belong to an explicit page edit and never run during warmed reading or rendering.
The first shading cache insertion allocates the dictionary's entry storage, keyed by the PDF shading dictionary. This storage belongs to the document's render cache.
The first shading lookup parses its dictionary and creates the PdfShading retained by the document's shading cache. Later recorded-page replay uses the completed recording.

The first shading lookup resolves its resource dictionaries and inserts the parsed shading into a dictionary cache. These paths use integer key or bucket storage; the sampled enclosing frame does not identify which nested array constructor ran.
Native wrappers created during soft-mask recording own SkiaSharp handle-lookup dictionaries. The observed generic dictionary type identifies that wrapper bookkeeping, not PDF object storage.
The first soft-mask insertion allocates dictionary entry storage keyed by the mask dictionary and current transform. The document's render cache retains the recorded mask.
Finishing the native soft-mask recording creates a managed backend owner for the SKPicture. The mask retains this disposable owner so native picture lifetime stays behind the drawing abstraction.

A cache miss records the soft-mask form with an owned child content interpreter. This isolates its parsing and graphics state from the outer page interpreter, and the completed mask recording is retained.

SkiaSharp registers the native wrappers made while recording the soft-mask form in its handle dictionary. The sampled node type identifies that handle-table entry; warm replay reuses the recorded mask.
Recording an uncached soft-mask form creates the PdfSoftMask result containing the completed picture, luminosity mode, backdrop and optional transfer table. The render cache retains this result.
SkiaSharp's handle dictionary uses weak references for native wrappers created while the soft-mask form is recorded. The mask itself retains the completed picture strongly.
Recording the uncached soft-mask form creates native picture wrappers. The completed recording is retained by the soft mask and released with the renderer's cached picture resources.
Starting the soft-mask picture recorder creates its native recording canvas wrapper. The recorder owns the canvas during recording and the cached mask owns the completed picture.
Recording the uncached soft-mask form creates the native drawing device's fill and stroke paints. The device owns and disposes these wrappers after recording.

The trace reports an object array while the uncached soft-mask form is resolved and recorded. This encloses lazy PDF object loading and native-wrapper setup; the stack does not identify the nested array constructor.

Resolving a new soft-mask form reads its resource dictionaries and inserts its recording into a dictionary cache. These paths use integer key or bucket arrays; the sampled enclosing frame does not resolve the nested array constructor.

The trace reports System.Object allocations while the uncached soft-mask form is resolved and recorded. This encloses lazy resource parsing and native-wrapper creation; the resolved stack does not identify the nested constructor of each System.Object.

Interpreting a fill detaches an immutable managed path containing an independent command snapshot. This owned contour replaces sharing native path state across the engine and backend; it is created during recording, not warm replay.

Interpreting a fill detaches the path builder into an owned Skia path wrapper before painting it into the page recording. The wrapper is disposed after the fill; warm picture replay does not detach paths.

The trace reports System.Object allocations under the fill operation that detaches, paints and disposes a native path. The resolved stack does not identify the nested System.Object constructor, so no particular native-wrapper bookkeeping object is claimed. This belongs to interpreting the uncached page.

Recording a form's bounding-box clip grows the managed command list and detaches an exact-sized command snapshot. The immutable clip owns its commands independently of the interpreter's reusable builder.
The backend converts the form's managed bounding-box contour to a temporary native path for clipping, then disposes the wrapper. The completed page recording retains the clip operation.

The trace reports System.Object allocations while recording a form's bounding-box clip and converting it to a native path. The resolved enclosing frame does not identify the nested object constructor.

Adding a rectangle appends its move, line and close commands to the managed builder. Its command list grows backing arrays while recording the uncached page; recorded-picture replay does not build rectangles.
Detaching creates the immutable managed path that owns an exact-sized command snapshot, then clears the reusable builder. This is first-recording path ownership, not warm picture replay.
Opening creates the owned object store for the new document. ColdOpenAndRender opens and disposes a fresh store on every operation; recorded-page replay does not open a store.

Opening creates an initial cross-reference table and the table populated while reading the file. The source creates both during each fresh document open; recorded-page replay does not construct cross-reference tables.
Opening reads the PDF version digits and Encoding.UTF8.GetString creates the stored version string. The version is read once for each new document.

Reading the cross-reference structure creates the document's object-slot array, sized to the final table. It replaces the temporary catalog-validation slots and retains parsed objects for this open document.

Cross-reference reading creates visited-section sets and parses trailer dictionaries, which use integer bucket and key arrays. The trace attributes these integer arrays to ReadStructure; it does not distinguish the nested collection or parser constructors.

Checking the trailer's Root reference creates an object-slot array sized to the cross-reference table before loading the catalog. This temporary opening cache is replaced by ReadStructure's final cache.

Parsing a stream object creates its PdfStream wrapper with the dictionary, source range and object identity. The object store retains the wrapper after first loading the stream; the fixture's bytes are not copied here.
Content-interpreter path builders own command-list wrappers created during the first page recording. The recorded page is replayed without rebuilding these lists.
A new content interpreter owns the graphics-state stack list used for save and restore during recording. Its list allocation is inlined into the cold render frame.
A new content interpreter owns the resource-stack list used while entering page and form content during recording. Warm replay does not instantiate this parsing state.

Cold page recording creates native drawing wrappers and their SkiaSharp handle dictionaries. The observed volatile-node array is backing storage for those handle tables; the enclosing Render frame includes inlined wrapper construction.
Cold recording traverses native-wrapper handle dictionaries during their setup and cleanup. The trace identifies the dictionary enumerator under Render; it does not resolve the inlined nested caller.

The first render of this newly opened document records its uncached page and creates the interpreters' graphics-state stack storage. Warm recorded-picture replay does not create interpreters or their stacks.
Cold recording creates native wrappers with SkiaSharp handle dictionaries. The observed table object belongs to that native-wrapper lookup storage and is attributed to the enclosing Render frame.
Recording the uncached page grows the interpreter's resource-stack backing array when page and form resources are entered. Replay uses the recorded result.
The first render creates content-interpreter path builders while recording the uncached page. These builders own the managed command construction state; cached picture replay does not create them.
Creating native wrappers for the uncached page records weak-reference bookkeeping in SkiaSharp's handle tables. The wrapper setup is inlined into the cold Render frame.
First recording resolves PDF resources and populates recording caches that use integer key or bucket storage. The trace attributes these arrays to Render without resolving the nested constructor.

The trace reports System.Object allocations under the first render's page recording and native-wrapper setup. The enclosing frame does not resolve the nested object constructor; warm replay separately measured zero library allocations.

A new picture recording owns an image-weight list used to account for its retained images. The list wrapper is created even when this transparency fixture records no images; replay reuses the completed picture.
Constructing the shading's native shader converts its managed color stops into a temporary Skia color array. The completed shader is cached; warm replay does not repeat this conversion.

The recording backend copies immutable managed commands into its reusable native path builder and detaches a temporary SKPath. The recording operation disposes that native wrapper after drawing or clipping.
The parsed shading owns a synchronization gate for first-use shader and mesh construction. The lock is created when the shading cache first parses this resource.
The child interpreter recording the uncached soft-mask form owns its marked-content visibility stack. The list wrapper belongs to that first recording, not cached mask replay.
Native wrappers created while recording the soft-mask form initialize SkiaSharp handle dictionaries. The observed volatile-node array is their handle-table backing storage.
Native wrappers created for the uncached soft-mask recording initialize SkiaSharp handle dictionaries. This sampled table object belongs to their native-handle lookup storage.

Cross-reference reading creates table location arrays and a stack of linked-section offsets, both using long arrays. The trace attributes the array to ReadStructure without resolving which nested table or traversal constructor ran.
